title_tag: Potassium Foods for Blood Pressure: What to Eat
og_title: Potassium-Rich Foods and Blood Pressure: What to Eat
desc: Potassium-rich foods can help lower blood pressure by balancing sodium. Here's which foods have the most, how much you need, and who should be careful.
h1_b: What to Eat, and How Much You Need
subhead: Sodium gets most of the blame for high blood pressure, but potassium matters just as much. Here's which foods actually deliver it, and where the evidence stands.
alt: Bananas, sweet potatoes, spinach and white beans arranged on a kitchen counter, foods rich in potassium for blood pressure
takeaways: Potassium helps the body excrete sodium and relax blood vessel walls, and diets higher in it are linked to lower blood pressure in large studies.
The best sources are whole foods: potatoes, beans, leafy greens, bananas, avocados, dairy and fish, not supplements, unless a doctor prescribes one.
Most adults in the US eat well below the recommended amount. A few consistent food swaps close most of that gap.
People with kidney disease or on certain blood pressure or heart medications need to be careful with potassium, since too much can be dangerous for them specifically.
Pairing potassium-rich foods with lower sodium intake, the approach behind the DASH diet, has more evidence behind it than either change alone.
pull: Potassium doesn't get the warning labels that sodium does. For blood pressure, the two minerals work as a pair, not a solo act.
body: Eating more potassium-rich foods, like potatoes, beans, bananas and leafy greens, is one of the better-supported ways to help lower blood pressure, alongside cutting back on sodium. Potassium helps the kidneys flush out excess sodium and eases tension in blood vessel walls. It isn't a replacement for medication or medical care, but for most healthy adults, it's a change worth making.

Blood pressure advice tends to focus on what to cut: less salt, less alcohol, less processed food. Potassium flips that script. It's a nutrient most people in the US actually need more of, and the food sources are things most grocery lists already include in smaller amounts. The harder part is knowing which foods actually move the needle and how much is enough.
How does potassium affect blood pressure?

Potassium and sodium work against each other inside the body. Sodium makes the body hold onto water, which raises the volume of fluid moving through blood vessels. Potassium helps the kidneys push extra sodium out through urine, and it also appears to relax the smooth muscle lining blood vessel walls, which can ease the pressure inside them. Large population studies, including research tied to the DASH eating pattern, link diets higher in potassium with measurably lower blood pressure, especially in people whose blood pressure is sensitive to sodium.

The effect isn't dramatic in any single meal. It builds over weeks of a consistently higher-potassium diet, the same way sodium's effect builds over weeks of a saltier one. For a deeper look at the sodium side of that equation, see our guide to lowering blood pressure naturally.
Which foods have the most potassium?
Whole, minimally processed foods carry the most potassium per serving, and several common ones beat the food most people associate with the mineral, the banana.

Potatoes and beans surprise a lot of people. Skin-on potatoes in particular carry more potassium than a banana, which is worth knowing if the diet already leans on potatoes as a starch. Dairy, fish and citrus round out the list without needing a single supplement pill.
How much potassium do you actually need?

Recommended intakes vary by age and sex, and the exact number has been revised over the years as research has evolved, so the safest move is checking the current figure on a source like the NIH Office of Dietary Supplements fact sheet rather than memorizing one number. What's consistent across every version of the guidance is that most American adults fall short of it, often by a wide margin, mainly because the modern diet leans heavily on processed food that's stripped of potassium during manufacturing while sodium is added back in.

That gap matters more than the exact target. Someone eating mostly fast food, packaged snacks and refined grains is likely getting well under half of what's recommended, regardless of which specific number applies to them. Closing even part of that gap with real food tends to move blood pressure in the right direction.
What about eating out, where you can't control the ingredients?

Restaurant meals make potassium harder to track, since there's no label to check, but a few patterns still hold. A grilled or baked protein with a side of vegetables or a baked potato beats a fried entree with fries almost every time, both for potassium and for the sodium that tends to ride along with heavily processed restaurant food. Salad bars and build-your-own bowl places make this easier, since beans, leafy greens and avocado are usually available as add-ons. Soup is a mixed bag: bean- and lentil-based soups can be a solid potassium source, but many restaurant and canned soups are also among the saltiest items on a menu, so it's worth asking or checking when sodium is the bigger concern that day.

Fast food is the hardest setting to get this right in, mostly because the menu skews toward refined bread, fried potatoes and processed meat, none of which carry much potassium. A side salad or a bean-based option, where available, is usually the better swap over fries, even if it isn't a perfect fix.
What foods are low in potassium that people eat instead?

White bread, white rice, most breakfast cereals, soda, and the bulk of packaged snack food carry little to no potassium, and many are high in sodium at the same time, which pushes the sodium-potassium balance in the wrong direction twice over. This isn't about guilt over any one food. It's about which swaps give the best return.
Swap a side of fries for a baked potato with the skin on
Swap white rice for beans or lentils a few times a week
Swap a sugary cereal for plain yogurt with fruit
Swap soda for a glass of orange juice or water with citrus
Add a serving of leafy greens or avocado to one meal a day
What does a potassium-rich day of eating actually look like?

Breakfast: plain yogurt with berries, or oatmeal with a sliced banana and a handful of walnuts. Lunch: a baked potato topped with black beans and salsa, or a spinach salad with chickpeas and a citrus vinaigrette. Dinner: baked salmon with roasted sweet potato and steamed broccoli, or a lentil and vegetable stew. Snacks: half an avocado with lime, a glass of orange juice, or a small handful of dried apricots.

None of that requires a special shopping list. It's mostly a matter of choosing the potato over the fries, the beans over the white rice, and the fruit over the chips, a handful of times a day rather than once in a while. Stacked across a week, those small swaps add up to a meaningfully different potassium total without feeling like a diet.
Is the sodium-to-potassium ratio more important than either number alone?

Some researchers argue that the ratio between the two minerals predicts blood pressure risk better than looking at sodium or potassium in isolation, since the two act on the same systems in opposite directions. A diet heavy in processed food tends to be both high in sodium and low in potassium at the same time, which stacks the ratio in the worst possible direction. A diet built around whole foods tends to correct both sides at once, since the same swaps, more vegetables and legumes, less packaged food, lower sodium while raising potassium together.

This is part of why cutting sodium alone sometimes produces smaller blood pressure changes than expected in research: if potassium intake stays low, only half of the lever gets pulled. Thinking in terms of the ratio, rather than chasing one number, is a more useful mental model for most people than memorizing a specific milligram target.
Does the DASH diet work better than potassium alone?

The research base is stronger for combining higher potassium with lower sodium than for either change by itself. The DASH diet, short for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, builds on exactly that pairing: more vegetables, fruit, beans, nuts and low-fat dairy, less red meat, sweets and sodium. Clinical trials testing DASH against a typical American diet found measurable drops in blood pressure within weeks, in some cases comparable to a low dose of blood pressure medication, though DASH is meant to complement medical care, not replace it. Our guide to the Mediterranean diet for beginners covers a closely related pattern with much of the same potassium-rich food base.
Can you get too much potassium from food?

For someone with healthy kidneys, it's hard to overdo potassium through food alone. The kidneys regulate the mineral efficiently and excess amounts are flushed out in urine. The real risk shows up in specific groups, covered in detail below, where the kidneys can't clear potassium normally or a medication changes how the body handles it. Supplements are a different story: high-dose potassium pills can push blood levels up quickly and should only be used under medical supervision.

Symptoms of genuinely high blood potassium, called hyperkalemia, can include muscle weakness, tingling, nausea or an irregular heartbeat, and it's generally picked up through a routine blood test rather than something people self-diagnose from symptoms alone. Anyone with kidney disease, heart failure, or taking medications that affect potassium should rely on their doctor's lab monitoring rather than guessing from how they feel.
Who should be careful with potassium-rich foods?

A few groups need to check with a doctor before deliberately increasing potassium intake. People with chronic kidney disease often can't clear excess potassium normally, and a buildup, called hyperkalemia, can affect heart rhythm. Certain blood pressure and heart medications change potassium handling too, including ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing diuretics; combining those with a sudden jump in potassium-rich foods, or with potassium supplements, can raise blood levels more than expected. Anyone in these groups should ask their doctor or a dietitian for a target that fits their specific situation rather than following general advice.

For everyone else, the food sources on this list are the safer, better-studied route compared with supplement pills, which is exactly why doctors tend to recommend food first. Our Heart Health hub covers related habits worth pairing with diet, including how many steps a day actually help your heart and what a healthy resting heart rate by age looks like.
How long before dietary changes affect blood pressure readings?

Studies testing DASH and similar potassium-rich eating patterns typically see measurable changes within two to four weeks of consistent eating, not days. Blood pressure also varies meal to meal and day to day for reasons unrelated to diet, including stress, sleep and how recently you've been active, so a single reading right after a potassium-rich meal won't show much. Anyone tracking progress should look at averages over a week or two, ideally with a home monitor, rather than any one number.
faq: Is a banana the best source of potassium?
No. A medium banana has around 420 mg, less than a baked potato with skin, white beans, spinach or lentils. It's a convenient snack, not the top source.
Can potassium supplements replace high blood pressure medication?

No. Potassium-rich food can support healthy blood pressure, but supplements should only be used under a doctor's guidance, and no diet change should replace a prescribed medication without medical advice.
Does cooking reduce the potassium in vegetables?
Boiling can leach some potassium into the water, especially with potatoes. Steaming, roasting or microwaving keeps more of it in the food.
Is coconut water a good source of potassium?
It contains some, typically less per serving than a potato, banana or cup of white beans, but it can be a reasonable low-calorie option between meals.
Can you take too much potassium from food if you're healthy?
It's uncommon with healthy kidneys, since they regulate and excrete excess potassium efficiently. The real caution applies to people with kidney disease or certain medications.
Do salt substitutes count as a potassium source?

Many salt substitutes use potassium chloride in place of some sodium, which can add a meaningful amount. They're not appropriate for people with kidney disease or on potassium-affecting medications without a doctor's okay.
How quickly does potassium lower blood pressure?
Studies on potassium-rich eating patterns like DASH generally show changes over two to four weeks of consistent intake, not after a single meal or day.
What are symptoms of getting too much potassium?

Muscle weakness, tingling, nausea or an irregular heartbeat can signal high blood potassium, though it's usually confirmed with a blood test rather than symptoms alone. This is rare from food in people with healthy kidneys.
